misconceptions.name: Stops after subtracting first cost
misconceptions.description: The child subtracts only the first cost mentioned and reports that difference as the final answer, ignoring the remaining costs that also need to be subtracted. [no predictor reproduces this answer, so it cannot be marked from the answer alone]
misconceptions.repair_hint: Use a checklist: tick off each cost after you subtract it, and count how many costs the problem lists before you start.
misconceptions.source: misconception_list · claude-haiku-4-5 · prompt 3bc886dc-8e92-4ff7-953d-21addc8fcbef

misconceptions.name: Subtracts costs in wrong order
misconceptions.description: The child subtracts the largest cost first, then the next largest, treating the sequence of subtraction as if order does not matter to the final answer—when place-value shifts or exchanging across different column positions produce different intermediates.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Use a place-value chart or number line to show that subtracting in a different sequence changes the path but the answer should stay the same; ask the child to check both orders.
misconceptions.source: misconception_list · claude-haiku-4-5 · prompt 3bc886dc-8e92-4ff7-953d-21addc8fcbef

misconceptions.name: Treats estimate as the final answer
misconceptions.description: The child rounds both numbers, calculates the estimate, then writes the estimate as the answer without working out the exact calculation.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Use the phrase 'estimate first, then calculate exact' to mark both steps as separate and both required.
misconceptions.source: misconception_list · claude-haiku-4-5 · prompt 3bc886dc-8e92-4ff7-953d-21addc8fcbef

misconceptions.name: Treats exchange as compensation
misconceptions.description: When asked about a regrouping claim (trading a ten for ten ones), the child explains it using compensation language—that moving between columns keeps things balanced—rather than recognising that the total stays the same because ten ones equals one ten.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Use place-value rods to show physically that one ten and ten ones represent the same amount; exchange is substitution, not compensation.
misconceptions.source: misconception_list · claude-haiku-4-5 · prompt 3bc886dc-8e92-4ff7-953d-21addc8fcbef

misconceptions.name: Treats friendly-number shortcut as column method
misconceptions.description: The child writes down the friendly-number compensation steps in column-addition format, mixing the conceptual strategy with formal regrouping, and loses track of when to apply the adjustment.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Ask the child to explain the friendly-number method in words first, without columns, then write the single adjusted answer.
misconceptions.source: misconception_list · claude-haiku-4-5 · prompt 3bc886dc-8e92-4ff7-953d-21addc8fcbef

misconceptions.name: Treats number wall as repeated column addition
misconceptions.description: In a number wall where each brick is the sum of the two below, the child writes out every single two-number addition as a column sum instead of using bridging or friendly-number shortcuts to find the top brick mentally.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Ask the child to explain their jumps on a number line instead of writing each sum; make it a speed challenge so bridging feels faster.
misconceptions.source: misconception_list · claude-haiku-4-5 · prompt 3bc886dc-8e92-4ff7-953d-21addc8fcbef

misconceptions.name: Counts a bundle as four
misconceptions.description: Misses the line across a bundle, so each bundle counts four: a bundle and three lines read as 7, not 8.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Say 'five' on the line across; make bundles of four sticks with a fifth laid across them.
misconceptions.source: Grade 1 educator's list of what was taught to September (Nimish, 2026-10-06)

misconceptions.name: Counts the line across as a sixth
misconceptions.description: Counts the four lines and then the line across as one more, so each bundle counts six: a bundle and three lines read as 9.
misconceptions.repair_hint: The line across is the fifth line, not an extra one: count a bundle 1, 2, 3, 4, 5.
misconceptions.source: Grade 1 educator's list of what was taught to September (Nimish, 2026-10-06)

misconceptions.name: Counts a bundle as one
misconceptions.description: Counts each bundle as a single line: a bundle and three lines read as 4.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Open a bundle into five sticks and count them; then count bundles in fives: 5, 10, 15.
misconceptions.source: Grade 1 educator's list of what was taught to September (Nimish, 2026-10-06)

misconceptions.name: Leaves out a group
misconceptions.description: Adds one group fewer than there are: 3 groups of 4 counted as 8, not 12.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Touch and count the groups first, then add one number for each group.
misconceptions.source: Grade 1 educator's list of what was taught to September (Nimish, 2026-10-06)

misconceptions.name: Gives one group, not all of them
misconceptions.description: Writes how many are in one group: 3 groups of 4 written as 4.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Ask 'how many in all?' and circle every group before counting.
misconceptions.source: Grade 1 educator's list of what was taught to September (Nimish, 2026-10-06)

misconceptions.name: Reads 'times as many' as 'more'
misconceptions.description: Adds the two numbers where a story says times as many: twice as many as 7 written as 9, three times as many as 6 written as 9.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Draw the first amount, then draw it again as many times as the story says; count them all.
misconceptions.source: goals/md2d1-multiplication-models.yaml (the multiplication & division taxonomy drafted 2026-10-09, B11 and B10)

misconceptions.name: Multiplies a partitioned tens digit as ones
misconceptions.description: Partitions a number and multiplies its tens (or hundreds) digit as if it were ones: 20 × 4 written as 8, so 23 × 4 = 2 × 4 + 3 × 4 = 20.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Say each part aloud as tens before multiplying: twenty times four is eighty, not eight
